behavioral_effects: None stated. An empty list is a claim that nothing observably changes.
compatibility_impact: The refresh response shape is unchanged. Both client call sites (api-client refreshAccessToken and the apiClient request path used by use-auth) now send X-Token-Refresh, so the transparent 401-retry flow and the WebSocket reconnect token refresh keep working; vitest covers accept and reject paths. Any future non-app caller of /api/auth/refresh must send the marker header.
reason: Security finding: the Next /api/auth/refresh route reads the HttpOnly refresh cookie and returns a fresh access token in its JSON body, so any script that can POST to it same-origin defeats the HttpOnly protection; gate it on Sec-Fetch-Site and a custom request header as defense in depth now that the uploaded-HTML execution vector is closed
rollback: git revert removes the gate and the client marker together; partial reverts would lock the app out of refreshing (gate without marker) and must not be cherry-picked.
security_impact: The refresh proxy no longer hands out access tokens to arbitrary same-origin POSTs: it requires the X-Token-Refresh marker header and rejects any request whose Sec-Fetch-Site metadata is not same-origin, so cross-site callers and sandboxed opaque-origin documents (the uploaded-content vector, already sandboxed in a prior session) get 403 before the cookie is read. Verified live: no marker 403, cross-site metadata 403, legitimate call 200. Residual accepted risk: a full same-origin XSS can still set the marker - unavoidable while the chat WebSocket design requires the access token in JS; the layered defenses (upload sandbox, CSP, this gate) reduce the paths to such an XSS.
summary: Require same-origin fetch metadata and an explicit client header on the auth refresh route
